cards.front: What do pre-drive checks cover, and what follows them?
cards.back: Pre-drive checks cover firm brakes, lit lamps, sound tires, and clean glass, with tinted rear glass demanding dual mirrors reaching two hundred feet, then park, seat, mirrors, clear view, locks, and belts.

cards.front: How should a driver back up safely?
cards.back: Backing starts with a walk-around for children, turns with an arm over the seat through the rear glass without trusting mirrors or cameras, rolls slowly, and uses a spotter when possible.

cards.front: Where are blind spots, and what do they require?
cards.back: Blind corners hide beside both rear flanks, need head turns before lane moves and passes, forbid riding inside others, and grow with vehicle size.

cards.front: In what order do the pre-drive checks run?
cards.back: Pre-drive checks run brakes, lamps, tires, glass, and dual mirrors past tint, then park, seat, mirrors, locks, belts.
cards.memory_hook: Car checks, then seat and belts

cards.front: How should you look while backing?
cards.back: Backing looks through glass with an arm turned, never trusting mirrors or cameras, and rolls slowly with spotters.

cards.front: Where do blind corners sit, and how do truck zones compare?
cards.back: Rear-flank corners hide from mirrors and need head turns, and truck zones dwarf car zones.

cards.front: How long do perception and reaction take, and how far does a car travel?
cards.back: Alert perception runs three-quarters to one second and reaction matches it, costing fifty-five feet at fifty miles per hour before braking starts.

cards.front: How far does braking take at fifty miles per hour, and how does speed change it?
cards.back: Braking alone spans one hundred fifty-eight feet at fifty miles per hour on dry grip, multiplies four, nine, and sixteen times with doubled, tripled, and quadrupled speed, and totals two hundred sixty-eight feet with perception and reaction.

cards.front: What is the minimum following gap, and when should it grow?
cards.back: Following holds four seconds minimum by marker counting, and stretches in rain, dim light, passes, loads, and uphill queues.

cards.front: Which vehicles call for a wider gap, and how far back stay from fire trucks?
cards.back: Gaps widen for fall-prone bikes, crossing-bound buses, hazmat haulers, and blind-backed rigs, fire trucks keep five hundred feet, and tailgated drivers slow rightward.

cards.front: How long do perception and reaction each take?
cards.back: Perception and reaction each run three-quarters to one second, costing fifty-five feet at fifty miles per hour

cards.front: What is the braking distance and total stopping distance at fifty miles per hour?
cards.back: Braking spans one hundred fifty-eight feet at fifty miles per hour, squares with doubled speed, and totals two hundred sixty-eight feet with human delays.

cards.front: How is the four-second gap measured, and when does it stretch?
cards.back: Four seconds minimum by marker count stretches for rain, dark, passes, loads, and hills.

cards.front: How far apart do trucks space, and how do intersections clear?
cards.back: Trucks and tows space three hundred feet outside cities and passes, and intersections halt at lines, yield after stops, scan both ways with a right glance, clear by arrival with right-side ties, and turn behind straight traffic.

cards.front: Who yields at driveways and at open crossings?
cards.back: Driveways yield to roads, walks, and bike lanes, and open crossings yield to occupants, state highways, paved roads, and oncoming left-turn conflicts.

cards.front: How does traffic move in a roundabout?
cards.back: Roundabouts circle one-way counterclockwise, yield entries to insiders and walkers, skip empty yields, forbid lane swaps and stops, signal exits, split straight-or-right right and straight-or-left-and-U left, and share with bikes.

cards.front: How far do you stay behind fire trucks and between trucks?
cards.back: Fire trucks keep five hundred feet, truck pairs keep three hundred, and tailgated drivers slow rightward.

cards.front: How do intersections clear when cars arrive together?
cards.back: Intersections clear by arrival with right-side ties, and two-way turners trail straight traffic.

cards.front: Who yields at driveways and open crossings?
cards.back: Driveways yield to everything, and open crossings yield to occupants, highways, pavement, and left-turn conflicts.

cards.front: What are the main roundabout rules?
cards.back: Roundabouts circle counterclockwise with entry yields, no swaps or stops, signaled exits, and lane-split multi rings.

cards.front: Who is barred from limited roads, and how do you enter them?
cards.back: Limited roads bar stops, lights, crossings, walkers, hitchhikers, bikes, carts, and small scooters, and entries check ramps, signal, accelerate, adjust, merge with yields, and never stop.

cards.front: How should you exit and cruise on a highway?
cards.back: Exits take the right lane with signals and ramp speeds, never last-minute, and cruisers plan mile-matched exits, keep right, shun medians and stops, and clear breakdowns within six hours.

cards.front: What highway habits does the handbook list?
cards.back: Highway drivers space out, never back ramps except past wrong-way signs and red reflectors, and rest when drowsy.

cards.front: What does the Move Over law require?
cards.back: Move Over shields lit workers and rigs plus flagged disabled cars, vacating lanes or slowing twenty under on wide roads, slowing twenty under on two-lanes, and crawling five where limits read twenty or less.

cards.front: Who may not use limited roads, and how do entries work?
cards.back: Limited roads bar walkers, bikes, and small scooters, and entries signal, accelerate, and merge with yields.

cards.front: How do exits work, and how soon must breakdowns be cleared?
cards.back: Exits signal right and slow on ramps, cruisers plan mile exits, and breakdowns clear pavement within six hours.

cards.front: When may a driver back on a ramp?
cards.back: Ramp backing is banned except past wrong-way signs and red reflectors, which force retreat.

cards.front: What speeds does the Move Over law require?
cards.back: Wide roads vacate lanes or slow twenty under, two-lanes slow twenty under, and twenty-limit roads crawl five.

cards.front: How should a car be parked along a road?
cards.back: Parking hugs roadside shoulders on the right except one-ways, parallels traffic with right wheels inside twelve inches, brakes with Park or Reverse, kills and locks with keys pocketed, and exits and reenters with checks, signals, and yields.

cards.front: How do you park on a hill?
cards.back: Hill parking rolls wheels from traffic into curbs, brakes, gears Park or Reverse downhill and First uphill, and kills the engine.

cards.front: Where is parking banned, and at what distances?
cards.back: Straight-in cars center clear of lanes, and parking bans cover walks, lanes, crossings, spans, tunnels, driveways, yellow curbs, signed zones, doubles, bare pavement, and hazards, with fifteen feet for hydrants, twenty for corners and stations, thirty for boxes and signs, and fifty for rails.

cards.front: Which way do wheels point when parking on hills?
cards.back: Hill wheels aim to curbs downhill, away uphill with curbs, and rightward uphill without.

cards.front: How close to the curb, and what else secures a parked car?
cards.back: Parking parallels right with wheels inside twelve inches, brakes geared, and keys pocketed.

cards.front: Which gear do you use parking downhill and uphill?
cards.back: Hills gear Park or Reverse downhill and First uphill with wheels curbed and brakes set.

cards.front: What are the no-parking distances?
cards.back: Bans clear fifteen feet for hydrants, twenty for corners and stations, thirty for boxes and signs, and fifty for rails.

cards.front: How do wheels point uphill with and without a curb?
cards.back: Hill wheels curb downhill, uncurb uphill with curbs, and swing right uphill without.

cards.front: How should a driver pass another vehicle?
cards.back: Passing signals, hangs back, checks and rooms out, horns by day and flashes by night, returns past visible tires with signals, clears before two hundred feet of oncoming, takes one car, and never speeds.

cards.front: Where is passing banned?
cards.back: Passing bans cover solid lines and zones, hills and curves under five hundred feet of sight, one hundred feet of crossings and spans, halted buses, and walker queues.

cards.front: What should a driver being passed do, and when is right-side passing allowed?
cards.back: Passed drivers hold speed, slide right, and cede the left lane to faster comers, while right-side passing needs two same-way lanes or a left-turning leader.

cards.front: Does right of way ever excuse a crash?
cards.back: Yield law assigns priority, yet every road user must still do everything to dodge crashes.

cards.front: What are the steps of a safe pass?
cards.back: Passes signal, room out, warn by horn or flash, return past visible tires, and clear before two hundred feet.

cards.front: Which places ban passing?
cards.back: Bans cover solids, short-sight hills and curves, one hundred-foot crossings, halted buses, and walker queues.

cards.front: What do passed drivers do, and when may you pass on the right?
cards.back: Passed drivers hold speed and slide right, and right-side passes need twin lanes or left-turning leaders.

cards.front: What do speed limits mean, and is there a ten-over buffer?
cards.back: Limits mark favorable-condition maximums demanding weather cuts, impact quadruples and nonuples with doubled and tripled speed, and no ten-over buffer exists.

cards.front: What are the standard speed limits?
cards.back: Standard limits read twenty for schools, thirty for towns, fifty-five for roads, and seventy for limited ways, while laggards must flow right with fifty minimum under seventy postings.

cards.front: How should you stop smoothly, and where do you drive on two lanes?
cards.back: Smooth stops scan rearward, coast off gas, and brake steadily alight, and two-lane drivers keep right except to pass.

cards.front: Which lanes do you use on roads with four or more lanes?
cards.back: Four-plus-lane roads stack right except to pass, and three- and five-lane centers turn left only.

cards.front: Who may use HOV lanes?
cards.back: HOV lanes serve doubled riders and decaled clean cars under diamond signs and buffers with gated entries.

cards.front: What do red reflectors on lane lines and edges mean?
cards.back: Red lane-line reflectors flag wrong-way travel needing instant correction, and red edge reflectors flag wrong ramps needing pullovers.

cards.front: How do you prepare for and signal a turn?
cards.back: Turns signal one hundred feet ahead including lane changes, never invite passes, hand-signal leftward, slow, lane up, and honor no-turn plates.

cards.front: Whom do turning drivers yield to, and which lane do they finish in?
cards.back: Turners yield bikes, walkers, and oncoming streams, hold proper lanes, finish rights in right lanes and lefts in any lawful lane, and skip last-minute cuts for the next corner.
cards.memory_hook: Rights finish in the right lane

cards.front: When and how do you make a three-point turn?
cards.back: Three-point turns suit narrow dead-ends only, run right-signal-sharp-left-stop then reverse-sharp-right then forward, and never touch curves, hills, highways, or U-ban spots.

cards.front: What do limits cap, and how does impact change with speed?
cards.back: Limits cap fair weather only, impacts square with speed, and no ten-over buffer shields tickets.

cards.front: What are the standard limits by zone and the minimum on seventy roads?
cards.back: Standards read twenty, thirty, fifty-five, and seventy by zone, while seventy postings floor at fifty.

cards.front: Which vehicles may use HOV lanes?
cards.back: HOV lanes double riders or decal clean cars behind diamond gates.

cards.front: How do lane-line and edge red reflectors differ?
cards.back: Red lane-line reflectors demand instant correction and red edge reflectors demand pullovers.

cards.front: Where do turns finish, and where are three-point turns barred?
cards.back: Turns finish rights right and lefts anywhere lawful, and three-point turns dodge curves, hills, and highways.

recap_hooks.text: Check brakes, lamps, tires and glass, then back slowly while looking through the rear glass and turning your head for blind spots.
At fifty miles per hour a stop takes about two hundred sixty-eight feet, so keep at least four seconds behind and more in poor conditions.
Intersections clear by arrival with ties to the right, driveways yield to everyone, and roundabouts run counterclockwise with yields on entry.
Enter limited roads by signaling, accelerating and merging without stopping, and under Move Over vacate a lane or slow twenty under.
Park within twelve inches of the curb, turn wheels correctly on hills, and keep fifteen feet from hydrants and fifty from rails.
Pass only one car at a time without speeding, never near crossings, hills or curves, and hold your speed when being passed.
Limits are fair-weather maximums with no ten-over buffer, keep right except to pass, and signal turns one hundred feet ahead.
